finding: In the largest sample found (6,029 adults wearing a 4-channel Muse headband, eyes closed), the standard deviation of log10 band power across people of the same age is about 0.21 to 0.36 log10 units (a factor of 1.6 to 2.3 in power per SD), roughly two to three times the SD of the age means; the numbers are read from a scatter plot, not printed.
numbers: Mean within-age SD of log10 band power (muV^2), read from Fig. 3 (approximate): theta 0.21-0.23 (all four channels); delta 0.24-0.25 at TP9/TP10, 0.32 at AF7/AF8; alpha about 0.22 at AF7/AF8, about 0.31 at TP9/TP10; beta 0.23-0.24 at TP9/TP10, 0.32 (AF8) and 0.36 (AF7). Between-age SD (SD of the age means) 0.07-0.20.
baseline: No baseline: spread of absolute log10 power across participants within each year of age (each participant's value averaged over up to five sessions).
subjects: 6,029 adults 18-88 years (Muse app users who opted into research; 22,386 sessions, 47% of sessions rejected for noise)
electrodes_band_window: AF7, AF8, TP9, TP10 referenced to Fpz; delta 0-2 Hz, theta 3-7 Hz, alpha 8-13 Hz, beta 14-30 Hz (1 Hz FFT bins, 220 Hz sampling); whole cleaned session (1-min eyes-closed category task and 3-min eyes-closed breath counting), 1.16 s epochs over 275 muV^2 rejected

source.authors: Hashemi A, Pino LJ, Moffat G, Mathewson KJ, Aimone C, Bennett PJ, Schmidt LA, Sekuler AB
source.title: Characterizing Population EEG Dynamics throughout Adulthood

evidence_location: Figure 3 (y-axis, 'Mean Within Age SD') and its legend; Results, paragraph before the weighted least-squares model; Methods, 'EEG recording and processing' and 'EEG measures'
quote: was much larger than the between-age variance, a trend seen across all channels for all measures
caveats: Values read off a plotted figure (resolution about 0.01 log10 units), not tabulated. Consumer 4-channel headband in uncontrolled settings, forehead reference, eyes closed during a task and meditation rather than plain rest; includes measurement noise and session-to-session variation, so it is an upper bound on the trait spread. Absolute power only; relative power is not analyzed.

finding: The classical normative-EEG result that absolute band power is approximately log-normal across healthy people, and relative power is normalized by the logit transform; this justifies describing between-person spread as an SD of log power, but the paper's abstract gives no SD values.
numbers: No numbers in the abstract; transformations only: log(x) for absolute power, log(x/(1-x)) for relative power.
baseline: Not applicable (distribution shape across a normative sample).
subjects: A sample of healthy individuals (n not in abstract)
electrodes_band_window: Broad-band spectral parameters, absolute and relative power (details not in abstract)

source.authors: Gasser T, Bächer P, Möcks J
source.title: Transformations towards the normal distribution of broad band spectral parameters of the EEG

evidence_location: Abstract
quote: For relative power the transformation log(x/(1-x)) was excellent in all regards
caveats: Supports the log-Gaussian modeling choice only. John et al. (1988) Science 239:162-169 (neurometrics) was also checked: its abstract states that healthy persons show only chance deviations beyond predicted ranges but gives no SD; full text not accessible.

finding: Largest twin study of resting power confirms that between-person differences in eyes-closed power are mostly stable, heritable traits (highest heritability around the alpha peak), but the abstract reports no SD or percentile of power.
numbers: None in abstract (heritability values only, not stated numerically there).
baseline: Not applicable.
subjects: 760 subjects: 142 monozygotic and 167 dizygotic twin pairs and siblings, two cohorts with mean ages 26.2 and 49.4 years
electrodes_band_window: 19 leads, eyes closed; 24 bins of 1 Hz from 1.0 to 25.0 Hz

source.authors: Smit DJ, Posthuma D, Boomsma DI, Geus EJ
source.title: Heritability of background EEG across the power spectrum

evidence_location: Abstract
quote: Generally, heritability was highest around the alpha peak frequency and lower in the theta and delta bands.
caveats: The task listed 'Smit DJA et al. (2005) Biological Psychology 71:271-287'; no such paper was found in Europe PMC; this Psychophysiology paper is the Smit 2005 heritability study. Full text not accessed.

finding: NOT FOUND: a tabulated SD (or 10th/90th percentile ratio, or CV) of log relative power across healthy adults. Only the ICC-based split of total variance (Ziogas 2026, test-retest entry) is available for relative power.
numbers: none
baseline: n/a
subjects: n/a
electrodes_band_window: n/a
evidence_location: Tried: Hashemi 2016 full text (absolute power only); Europe PMC searches for open-access normative databases (Ko et al. 2021 Front Neurosci 15:766781, 1,289 subjects, reports no SD values in text; HarMNqEEG, Li et al. 2022 NeuroImage 256:119190, closed, norms are per-frequency log-spectra in figures); John 1988, Smit 2005 and Gasser 1982 abstracts.
caveats: A usable derived route: total SD of log power from Hashemi 2016 (about 0.21-0.36) times sqrt(ICC) from a test-retest study gives the stable between-person part, and times sqrt(1-ICC) the within-person part.

finding: Classic adult test-retest study: broad-band power features correlate 0.92 across a 5 min interval and 0.84 across 12-16 weeks; absolute and relative power are equally reliable by correlation, but relative power has smaller percent test-retest differences; 60 s of data beats 40 or 20 s.
numbers: Pearson r averaged over broad-band features: 0.92 (5 min retest), 0.84 (12-16 week retest); 'essentially no difference' between absolute and relative power; percent differences lower for relative than absolute power and lower for 60 s than 40 or 20 s records (values in body not accessed).
baseline: Same person, same eyes-closed resting condition, repeated after 5 min and after 12-16 weeks.
subjects: 19 healthy adults
electrodes_band_window: Montage not in abstract; FFT on visually edited segments totaling 60, 40 or 20 s

source.authors: Salinsky MC, Oken BS, Morehead L
source.title: Test-retest reliability in EEG frequency analysis

evidence_location: Abstract (per-band tables in body not accessed)
quote: averaged 0.92 over the 5 min retest interval and 0.84 over the 12-16 week interval
caveats: Per-band values and the percent differences (the within-person spread) are in the body, which is paywalled; no open copy found.

finding: Recent open-access study with the per-band intraclass correlations the site needs: over 14 days in 90 young adults, ICC(2,1) for log10 absolute power averaged over 64 electrodes is 0.66 (delta) to 0.88 (alpha), and for relative power 0.64 (gamma) to 0.86 (alpha); split-half consistency within a session is 0.93-0.98.
numbers: Adults (Table 5), test-retest ICC(2,1) [95% CI]: absolute delta 0.66 [0.51, 0.76], theta 0.77 [0.66, 0.85], alpha 0.88 [0.82, 0.92], beta 0.81 [0.72, 0.87], gamma 0.75 [0.64, 0.83]; relative delta 0.75 [0.64, 0.83], theta 0.80 [0.71, 0.87], alpha 0.86 [0.79, 0.91], beta 0.79 [0.70, 0.86], gamma 0.64 [0.49, 0.75]. Split-half (two 90 s halves, Spearman-Brown) 0.93-0.98 absolute, 0.87-0.97 relative. Children (Table 1, n = 36, about 60 days apart): absolute delta 0.77, theta 0.75, alpha 0.81, beta 0.76, gamma 0.54; relative delta 0.81, theta 0.61, alpha 0.84, beta 0.80, gamma 0.59.
baseline: Same person, two eyes-open resting recordings 14.13 days (SD 0.77) apart (adults); 59.69 days (SD 22.08) apart (children).
subjects: 90 adults (58 female, 18-40 years, mean 28.96; ICC computed on 85) and 36 children (9-15 years)
electrodes_band_window: 64-channel sponge RNet (Brain Products), reference Cz; absolute power log10-transformed and relative power (percent of 0.5-80 Hz total), averaged over all electrodes; delta 1-4, theta 4-8, alpha 8-14, beta 14-30, gamma 30-75 Hz; 180 s eyes open fixating a cross

source.authors: Ziogas A, Ruch S, Skieresz NH, Marca SC, Rothen N, Reber TP
source.title: Test-retest reliability analysis of resting-state EEG measures and their association with long-term memory in children and adults

evidence_location: Results 3.2, Table 5 (adults) and Results 3.1.2.1, Table 1 (children); Methods 2.2.3.1 for band definitions and log transform
caveats: Power averaged over all 64 electrodes, so site-specific ICCs are not given; a language-learning intervention occurred between sessions; eyes open only. ICC implies within-person variance = (1 - ICC) of total variance, e.g. 12% for alpha absolute power.

finding: Over twelve years, individual posterior alpha amplitude at rest still correlates 0.72 (full sample) to 0.85 (adults), showing that the between-person part of alpha power is largely a lifelong trait.
numbers: Overall (eyes closed plus open) posterior alpha amplitude: Spearman-Brown rSB = .834, Pearson r = .718 (full sample); adults rSB = .918, r = 0.848. Net alpha (closed minus open), adults: rSB = .750, r = .600. Asymmetry, adults: rSB = .728, r = .573.
baseline: Same person, two resting sessions 12 +/- 1.1 years apart.
subjects: 70 participants (29 male; 46 adults at first session)
electrodes_band_window: Reference-free current source density with PCA; posterior alpha amplitude (band limits not in abstract); eyes closed and eyes open resting EEG

source.authors: Tenke CE, Kayser J, Alvarenga JE, Abraham KS, Warner V, Talati A, Weissman MM, Bruder GE
source.title: Temporal stability of posterior EEG alpha over twelve years

evidence_location: Abstract (Results)
quote: Overall alpha was stable for the full sample (Spearman-Brown [rSB] = .834, Pearson's r = .718)
caveats: The task cited this as 2017; the journal issue is 2018. Sample drawn from a family study of depression risk; CSD-PCA alpha amplitude, not band power at a single electrode. Author manuscript in PMC (PMC5976526) but XML not served.

finding: Monthly recordings over nine months in women: each woman's pattern of absolute power across sites and bands correlates above 0.89 with her own later recordings; group stability was better with eyes closed than open, and poorest for eyes-open alpha.
numbers: Within-subject reliability r > 0.89 for all subjects and parameters (absolute power and coherence); inter-session stability higher with eyes closed, poorer with eyes open especially in alpha (values in body).
baseline: Same person, resting eyes open and eyes closed, once a month for nine months.
subjects: Healthy women (n not in abstract)
electrodes_band_window: Central and posterior regions; bands not in abstract

source.authors: Corsi-Cabrera M, Galindo-Vilchis L, del-Río-Portilla Y, Arce C, Ramos-Loyo J
source.title: Within-subject reliability and inter-session stability of EEG power and coherent activity in women evaluated monthly over nine months

evidence_location: Abstract
quote: Within-subject reliability was very high (r>0.89) for all subjects and EEG parameters.
caveats: The r > 0.89 is a profile correlation across sites and bands within a person, not an ICC of one band across people; per-band stability values are in the paywalled body.

finding: Over 25-62 months, the within-person change in absolute power and alpha mean frequency, expressed in z-units of a normative database, is smaller than the spread across people; absolute power had the least moment-to-moment variability.
numbers: No numeric values in abstract (SDs of test-retest differences in normative z-units are in the body).
baseline: Same person, qEEG repeated 25-62 months later; all values z-scored against a normal database.
subjects: 45 healthy adult volunteers
electrodes_band_window: Absolute and relative power, asymmetry, coherence, mean and peak frequency, entropy (montage and bands not in abstract)

source.authors: Kondacs A, Szabó M
source.title: Long-term intra-individual variability of the background EEG in normals

evidence_location: Abstract
quote: was less than the inter-individual variability in the normal population
caveats: This is the one candidate that directly reports within-person spread in units of between-person spread, but the numbers are in the paywalled body; no open copy found. Gasser, Bächer, Steinberg 1985 (EEG Clin Neurophysiol 60(4):312-319, doi 10.1016/0013-4694(85)90005-7; population and retest interval not in abstract) adds, from its abstract only, that delta power is least reliable, alpha most, and that 20 s of EEG suffices to tame the inherent random variability.

finding: Within a 10 min resting recording, the power of single 4 s epochs scatters with a coefficient of variation of about 0.4-0.8 depending on band (alpha the most variable, beta the least), the CV falls as 1/sqrt(number of epochs), and there is a slow drift toward the end of the recording (alpha and beta down, delta and theta up).
numbers: CV of 4 s epoch power: 0.49-0.67 (delta), 0.53-0.58 (theta), 0.58-0.76 (alpha), 0.37-0.49 (beta); alpha peak frequency CV 0.09-0.12. CV inversely proportional to sqrt(sample size). Lengthening the recording from 40 to 400 s increased CV by 36% (alpha), 41% (beta), 29% (delta), 35% (theta) while the standard error of the mean fell by 55-60%.
baseline: Scatter of epoch power about the subject's own mean within one session (no between-condition baseline); drift relative to the start of the 10 min recording.
subjects: 57 normal subjects
electrodes_band_window: Sites not in abstract; delta, theta, alpha, beta bands and alpha peak frequency; 4 s epochs; protocol of repeated 5 s eyes-open then 55 s eyes-closed cycles for 10 min

source.authors: Maltez J, Hyllienmark L, Nikulin VV, Brismar T
source.title: Time course and variability of power in different frequency bands of EEG during resting conditions

evidence_location: Abstract (ranges as printed; what each range spans, sites or conditions, is not stated in the abstract)
quote: 0.49-0.67 (delta), 0.53-0.58 (theta), 0.58-0.76 (alpha), 0.37-0.49 (beta) and 0.09-0.12 for the alpha peak frequency
caveats: CV is of linear power, not log power; the size of the end-of-recording drift is in the body (paywalled). A CV of 0.6 for a 4 s epoch is consistent with a chi-square-like estimate with few degrees of freedom plus true waxing and waning.

finding: Within one 180 s eyes-open session, band power from the first and second 90 s halves agrees very closely (split-half reliability 0.93-0.98 for log absolute power), i.e. minute-scale drift is small compared with the between-person spread.
numbers: Adults, split-half reliability (Spearman-Brown) at T1/T2: absolute delta 0.96/0.93, theta 0.95/0.97, alpha 0.97/0.98, beta 0.98/0.98, gamma 0.95/0.95; relative delta 0.93/0.87, theta 0.91/0.93, alpha 0.94/0.95, beta 0.95/0.97, gamma 0.92/0.96.
baseline: First versus second 90 s half of the same recording.
subjects: 90 adults, 18-40 years
electrodes_band_window: 64 channels averaged; delta 1-4, theta 4-8, alpha 8-14, beta 14-30, gamma 30-75 Hz; 2 x 90 s eyes open

source.authors: Ziogas A, Ruch S, Skieresz NH, Marca SC, Rothen N, Reber TP
source.title: Test-retest reliability analysis of resting-state EEG measures and their association with long-term memory in children and adults

evidence_location: Table 5 (split-half columns) and its note
quote: Split-half reliability was calculated with the Spearman-Brown-Correction (between the two halves of 90 seconds segments).
caveats: A correlation across people, so it says that halves rank people the same way; it does not give the size of within-person drift directly.

finding: The only direct measurement of 'clean' versus contaminated scalp power: with complete neuromuscular blockade, power above 20 Hz fell by 10- to 200-fold depending on site, so most scalp power above 20 Hz in a relaxed, awake person is muscle.
numbers: 10- to 200-fold differences in power at frequencies above 20 Hz, paralysed versus unparalysed (per-site and per-frequency values in body figures).
baseline: Same two people awake, relaxed and doing cognitive tasks, before and during complete neuromuscular blockade (cisatracurium), dominant arm spared.
subjects: 2 subjects
electrodes_band_window: Multi-channel scalp EEG (montage in body); spectra across the full band, contamination from about 20 Hz upward

source.authors: Whitham EM, Pope KJ, Fitzgibbon SP, Lewis T, Clark CR, Loveless S, Broberg M, Wallace A, DeLosAngeles D, Lillie P, Hardy A, Fronsko R, Pulbrook A, Willoughby JO
source.title: Scalp electrical recording during paralysis: quantitative evidence that EEG frequencies above 20 Hz are contaminated by EMG

evidence_location: Abstract (Results); per-site spectra in body figures not accessed
quote: with 10- to 200-fold differences in the power of frequencies above 20 Hz during paralysis
caveats: Only two subjects, so the between-person range is unknown; the factor is for 'above 20 Hz' as a whole, and the 13-20 Hz part of beta is less affected (see the review entry). Full text paywalled; CORE and Europe PMC copies blocked.

finding: A review summarizes the paralysis data for central electrodes (far from the muscles): contamination begins at about 20 Hz, with roughly 5 times more power at 40 Hz and 10 times more at 80 Hz without paralysis, and much larger factors at the edge of the montage.
numbers: Central electrodes: ~5 times more power at 40 Hz and ~10 times more at 80 Hz in the non-paralyzed state; contamination 'started around 20 Hz'; maximal at the edges of the montage.
baseline: Unparalysed versus paralysed resting EEG in the same people (Whitham et al. 2007, 2008).
subjects: Review of Whitham et al. 2007 (2 subjects) and 2008 (4 paralysed subjects)
electrodes_band_window: Central scalp electrodes; 20-80 Hz

source.authors: Muthukumaraswamy SD
source.title: High-frequency brain activity and muscle artifacts in MEG/EEG: a review and recommendations

evidence_location: Section 'The relationship between EMG and MEG/EEG', paragraph on neuromuscular blockade
quote: at 40 Hz there was ~5 times more power in the non-paralyzed state
caveats: Secondary source; the primary per-frequency curves are in Whitham 2007 Fig. 4-6 (not accessed). Implies the 13-30 Hz beta band at central sites is contaminated by a factor between about 1 (at 20 Hz) and 5 (at 40 Hz) in a relaxed person.

finding: Follow-up paralysis study quantifies brain-to-muscle power ratios at central leads: with a surface Laplacian the muscle part is under one sixth of the brain signal above 30 Hz (B:M > 6), which it calls two to three times better than a common average reference, so a conventional CAR recording at central leads has roughly 2-3 times as much brain as muscle power above 30 Hz.
numbers: B:M > 6 above 30 Hz in central scalp leads (surface Laplacian); Laplacian 'two to three times better signal detection than CAR' (so CAR B:M about 2-3, derived); M defined as the power difference before minus after paralysis.
baseline: Power after paralysis (brain, B) versus before paralysis (brain plus muscle, B+M), same subjects, passive and active tasks.
subjects: Awake subjects recorded with and without complete neuromuscular blockade (n not in abstract)
electrodes_band_window: Central and pericentral leads; left-ear reference, CAR and three Laplacian estimators; up to 600 Hz, ratios quoted above 30 Hz

source.authors: Fitzgibbon SP, Lewis TW, Powers DM, Whitham EW, Willoughby JO, Pope KJ
source.title: Surface Laplacian of central scalp electrical signals is insensitive to muscle contamination

evidence_location: Abstract
quote: B:M > 6 above 30 Hz in central scalp leads
caveats: The CAR figure is my inference from 'two to three times better'; the per-band table is in the paywalled body. Ratios are for above 30 Hz, not 13-30 Hz.

finding: Mild deliberate tension: with 15% of maximum frontalis or temporalis contraction, EMG is statistically detectable even near the vertex above 12 Hz on average (above 8 Hz in some people); frontal EMG spectra peak at 20-30 Hz, i.e. inside the beta band, and at Fp/AF sites the 15% contraction raises 20-30 Hz amplitude several-fold while at Fz/Cz the spectra barely move; the paper gives spectra and R2 maps, no per-site power ratios in text.
numbers: Average spectra (Fig. 4, 25 subjects, CAR): at Fp1/Fp2 the 15% frontalis contraction curve lies roughly 3-4 times above the relaxation curve at 20-30 Hz (amplitude, read from the plot; about 10x in power), at Fz, FCz and Cz the relaxation and 15% curves nearly coincide at 20-30 Hz. Weak and moderate (15 and 30%) contractions affect 5-10 to 200 Hz at facial and anterior sites and 15-20 to 200 Hz at central sites. Analyzed data per subject averaged 58.9 s relaxation, 49.1 s at 15%, 52.4 s at 30%, 52.8 s at 70%.
baseline: Same person, 'relaxation' (eyes open, cursor task) versus contraction at 15, 30, 70 and 100% of the person's EMG range.
subjects: 25 healthy adults (Experiment 2; 10 in Experiment 1)
electrodes_band_window: 64 scalp electrodes (earlobe reference, re-referenced to CAR) plus 4 facial EMG sites; 1 Hz FFT bins 0-100 Hz (Experiment 2, 256 Hz sampling); trial-wise spectra averaged

source.authors: Goncharova II, McFarland DJ, Vaughan TM, Wolpaw JR
source.title: EMG contamination of EEG: spectral and topographical characteristics

evidence_location: Abstract; Results 3.1-3.2 and Fig. 3 and Fig. 4 (amplitude spectra per site); Discussion 4.2 and 4.4
quote: EMG was detectable (P<0.001) near the vertex at frequencies >12 Hz in the average data
caveats: The paper reports R2 (variance explained by contraction level) maps and spectra, not power ratios; my Fp versus Fz/Cz factors are rough readings of small panels at a shared 0-20 muV scale. Relaxation here still contains resting EMG (no paralysis). Open PDF at neurotechcenter.org (Wadsworth).

finding: NOT FOUND: the window-to-window variability of the muscle-to-brain beta ratio in a relaxed sitter (no source reports an SD or CV of EMG contamination across epochs).
numbers: none
baseline: n/a
subjects: n/a
electrodes_band_window: n/a
evidence_location: Tried: Goncharova 2003 full text (gives only mean spectra and R2 maps), Whitham 2007/2008 and Fitzgibbon 2013/2015 abstracts (paywalled bodies), McMenamin et al. 2010 NeuroImage 49(3):2416-2432 (PMC2818255; Europe PMC XML returns server error, PDF render blocked).
caveats: Maltez 2004's within-session CV of beta power (0.37-0.49 per 4 s epoch) necessarily includes EMG fluctuations and could serve as an upper bound.

finding: Study closest to the request: in 31 resting adults, uncorrected blinks and eye movements had substantial 'general' effects (mean shifts) on power across the whole spectrum at single sites, but 'differential' effects (changes in the rank order of people) in alpha and beta only at the frontopolar sites; numeric effect sizes are in the paywalled body.
numbers: No numbers in abstract (effect sizes per band and site are in the body's tables).
baseline: Data portions with versus without ocular artifacts, same people, eyes open and eyes closed rest.
subjects: 31 participants
electrodes_band_window: EEG and EOG, resting eyes open and closed; broadband delta, theta, alpha, beta (limits in body)

source.authors: Hagemann D, Naumann E
source.title: The effects of ocular artifacts on (lateralized) broadband power in the EEG

evidence_location: Abstract (Results)
quote: blinks and eye movements exerted substantial general effects on the whole EEG spectrum
caveats: No open copy found (publisher, library and index pages only).

finding: At frontal electrodes the ocular contribution to measured low-frequency activity exceeds the cerebral signal itself, and the person-to-person variation in EOG power inflates the between-subject variance of uncorrected frontal EEG.
numbers: No numbers in abstract.
baseline: Uncorrected versus EOG-corrected spectral parameters, same recordings.
subjects: 15 healthy controls and 17 schizophrenic patients
electrodes_band_window: Frontal region; bipolar vertical and horizontal EOG; slow-frequency power

source.authors: Gasser T, Ziegler P, Gattaz WF
source.title: The deleterious effect of ocular artefacts on the quantitative EEG, and a remedy
source.venue: European Archives of Psychiatry and Clinical Neuroscience

evidence_location: Abstract
quote: the influence of ocular artefacts on the measured electrical activity in the frontal region is larger than the cerebral potentials
caveats: Qualitative statement; small clinical sample. Gasser, Sroka, Möcks 1985 (EEG Clin Neurophysiol 61(2):181-193, doi 10.1016/0013-4694(85)91058-2) adds from its abstract that eye movements transfer into the EEG best at low frequencies and blink gains peak in the theta band, with high random variability of individual gain functions.

finding: Spontaneous blink rate in 150 healthy people: 17 per minute at rest, 26 during conversation, 4.5 while reading.
numbers: Mean blink rate: 17 blinks/min resting quietly; 26 blinks/min talking; 4.5 blinks/min reading (-55.08% versus rest while reading, +99.70% during conversation); log-normal distribution across people.
baseline: Rest condition versus reading and conversation, same people, videotaped.
subjects: 150 healthy volunteers (70 male, 80 female; 35.9 +/- 17.9 years, range 5-87)
electrodes_band_window: Video blink counting, not EEG

source.authors: Bentivoglio AR, Bressman SB, Cassetta E, Carretta D, Tonali P, Albanese A
source.title: Analysis of blink rate patterns in normal subjects

evidence_location: Abstract
quote: Mean BR at rest was 17 blinks/min, during conversation it increased to 26
caveats: Rest here is sitting quietly with eyes open; eyes-closed recordings have essentially no blinks.

finding: Blink statistics measured from the EEG/EOG itself in more than 2,000 laboratory datasets: average blink rates of 19.6-22.6 per minute, and a blink duration of about 0.12 s from eyelid crossing the pupil (half-maximum) or about 0.3 s for the full base-to-base EEG deflection.
baseline: Dataset averages across tasks (driving simulation, shooting, BCI tasks); no rest baseline.
subjects: Four EEG collections, more than 2,000 datasets from eight laboratories (subject counts per collection in the paper)
electrodes_band_window: Blinks detected on vertical EOG or a frontal channel (Fpz, Fp1, AF7, ...); durations from blink landmarks on the low-pass filtered signal

source.authors: Kleifges K, Bigdely-Shamlo N, Kerick SE, Robbins KA
source.title: BLINKER: Automated Extraction of Ocular Indices from EEG Enabling Large-Scale Analysis

evidence_location: Results, 'Analysis of blink rate' (Table 2) and 'Blink duration' (Table 3)
quote: Average blink rates over the collection ranged from 19.6 to 22.6 blinks/min
caveats: Task EEG, not rest; automated detection; the 'base' duration is the one that matters for how long a blink corrupts a frontal EEG window. No measured value for how much blinks add to frontal delta/theta power was found: Hagemann 2001 body paywalled; VanderWerf et al. 2003 J Neurophysiol 89(5):2784-2796 (blink kinematics) blocked.

finding: Within-subject reference for the SEED emotion dataset: a linear SVM on differential-entropy (log band power) features from 62 channels classifies positive/neutral/negative film emotions at 83.99% (DBN 86.08%) when trained and tested on different film clips of the same person's session.
numbers: Mean accuracy (SD) across 15 subjects x 2 sessions, three classes (chance 33.3%): DBN 86.08% (8.34%), SVM 83.99% (9.72%), LR 82.70% (10.38%), KNN 72.60% (13.16%). Train on 9 film clips, test on the other 6 of the same experiment.
baseline: Chance 33.3% (three equally sized classes); training and test from the same person and same recording day.
subjects: 15 subjects (SJTU students), each recorded twice a few days apart
electrodes_band_window: 62-channel ESI Neuroscan cap; DE features in delta 1-3, theta 4-7, alpha 8-13, beta 14-30, gamma 31-50 Hz from non-overlapping 1 s windows (310 features)

source.authors: Zheng W-L, Lu B-L
source.title: Investigating Critical Frequency Bands and Channels for EEG-Based Emotion Recognition with Deep Neural Networks
source.venue: IEEE Transactions on Autonomous Mental Development

evidence_location: Abstract; Section V.A and Table III; Section IV.D (train/test split)
quote: The average accuracies of DBN, SVM, LR, and KNN are 86.08%, 83.99%, 82.70%, and 72.60%
caveats: 'Within-subject' here is a within-session split by film clip, so it also benefits from same-day electrode placement; the companion paper below uses the same features and data for the cross-subject case.

finding: Same lab, same SEED data and features: a generic classifier trained on 14 people and tested on the 15th drops to 56.73% (from about 84% within-person), with a between-person SD of 16%; transfer learning recovers part of the gap (TPT 76.31%).
numbers: Leave-one-subject-out mean accuracy (SD), three classes: generic linear SVM 0.5673 (0.1629); KPCA 0.6128 (0.1462); TCA 0.6364 (0.1488); T-SVM 0.7253 (0.1400); TPT 0.7631 (0.1589) (Table 1).
baseline: Chance 33.3%; the within-subject result of 83.99% (SVM) in Zheng and Lu 2015 is the calibrated comparison.
subjects: 15 subjects (SEED), leave-one-subject-out
electrodes_band_window: 62 channels; DE features in five bands (delta 1-3, theta 4-7, alpha 8-13, beta 14-30, gamma 31-50 Hz) from non-overlapping 1 s windows

source.authors: Zheng W-L, Lu B-L
source.title: Personalizing EEG-Based Affective Models with Transfer Learning
source.venue: Proceedings of the Twenty-Fifth International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence (IJCAI-16)

evidence_location: Abstract; Section 4 and Table 1

finding: Independent cross-subject study on two public datasets: with leave-one-subject-out SVMs on a broad feature set, binary emotion recognition reaches 59.06% on DEAP (high versus low valence) and 83.33% on SEED (positive versus negative), against 50% chance.
numbers: DEAP: best mean accuracy 59.06% (AUC 0.605), no feature selection 0.5773-0.5594 depending on method (SD 0.08-0.10); SEED: 78.44% (SD 11.19%) without feature selection, 83.33% (SD 10.16%) with RFE selecting 130 features.
baseline: Chance 50% (two classes); no within-subject comparison in this paper.
subjects: DEAP: 32 subjects (17 male, 27.2 +/- 4.4 years), 32 channels; SEED: 15 subjects (7 male, 23.27 +/- 2.37 years), 62 channels
electrodes_band_window: 18 feature types (time-frequency and dynamical) in theta, alpha, beta, gamma from 1 min segments; leave-one-subject-out

finding: Workload: cross-participant (zero data from the test person) classification of low versus high Multi-Attribute Task Battery workload reached 0.77-0.87 accuracy depending on window length and network, and the paper's literature review gives the classic within-versus-across comparison of Gevins et al. 1998 (94% individually trained versus 83% group classifier).
numbers: Table 2, mean cross-participant accuracy, cross-validated group model, MPCRNN: 0.791 (5 s), 0.820 (10 s), 0.850 (20 s), 0.868 (30 s); other architectures 0.635-0.862; chance 0.5. Cited Gevins et al. 1998: group classifier 83% versus 94% for individually trained models; Gevins' own abstract: high versus low load discriminated at better than 95% within subject.
baseline: Chance 50% (two workload levels, balanced); leave-one-participant-out.
subjects: 8 participants (MATB, 5 training days, low and high difficulty)
electrodes_band_window: EEG sequences of 5, 10, 20 or 30 s (electrode count in body); Gevins 1998: 8 participants, spectral features, working-memory tasks

source.authors: Hefron R, Borghetti B, Schubert Kabban C, Christensen J, Estepp J

evidence_location: Table 2 (cross-participant accuracies); Section 1.1.2 (Gevins comparison); Gevins A, Smith ME, Leong H, McEvoy L, Whitfield S, Du R, Rush G (1998) Human Factors 40(1):79-91, doi 10.1518/001872098779480578, abstract
quote: The mean classification accuracy for the group classifier was 83% which represented a significant reduction from the 94% accuracy
caveats: The 94%/83% pair is quoted from Hefron's review of Gevins 1998, whose own abstract says 'better than 95%' within subject and only 'statistically significant' for new participants; Gevins full text not accessed. Hefron gives no within-participant run of its own networks. Roy et al. 2016 (J Neural Eng 13(2):026019, not 046019) is within-subject only: spectral chain 60%, ERP chain 91%, 20 participants. Lan et al. 2019 (IEEE TCDS) and Jiménez-Guarneros and Gómez-Gil 2020 were not accessible or not found in Europe PMC.
